units.blurb: Greet people by the hour, say thank you, and introduce yourself.

steps.body: Indonesian greetings are built from selamat ("safe, well") plus the part of the day. There is no single "hello" you use all day — people pick the one that matches the clock.
steps.title: Selamat + time of day

steps.why: Sore runs from roughly 3pm until it gets dark.

steps.body: Terima kasih is the full form; makasih is the everyday short one. The standard reply is sama-sama — literally "same-same".
steps.title: Thank you

steps.why: banyak ("a lot") goes after the thing it strengthens.
Sama-sama is the standard "you're welcome".

steps.body: Permisi is "excuse me" when you pass someone, enter a room or get a seller's attention. Maaf is "sorry" — for apologies, and for softening bad news.
steps.title: Permisi and maaf

steps.why: Malam is night — used once it's dark.
Bu (for women) and Pak (for men) are added constantly — leaving them out sounds blunt.

steps.body: "My name" is nama saya — noun first, owner second. Indonesian puts the owner after the thing owned, the opposite of English.
steps.title: Nama saya…

steps.why: No word for "is", and the owner follows the noun: name–my–Rina.

steps.prompt: Ask a new friend their name, casually:
steps.why: Indonesian asks siapa ("who"), not apa. -mu is the casual "your" and sticks to the noun.

steps.body: Saya dari… means "I'm from…" with no verb at all. For where you live, use tinggal di ("live at").
steps.title: Where you're from, where you live

steps.why: tinggal di = live in. The verb stays as it is.
senang = glad, bertemu = to meet. Formal; with friends, salam kenal is enough.
juga = "too", and it goes at the end.

tolong = please (do this for me), tunggu = wait, sebentar = a moment.

units.title: First words

units.blurb: Subject · verb · object, pronouns, no "to be", and describers that follow.

steps.body: Indonesian sentences run subject, verb, object — and the verb never changes. No -s, no past tense ending, nothing to conjugate for who is doing it.
steps.title: Same order as English

steps.why: Subject, verb, object — minum for drinking, makan for eating.

steps.body: saya is the safe "I"; aku is for friends. dia covers he and she. The big one: kita includes the person you're talking to, kami does not.
steps.title: Pronouns

steps.prompt: You're telling your friend "we're going" — the two of you. Pick:
steps.why: kita includes the listener. Saying kami here means "us, not you" and sounds like you're leaving them behind.
dia is he or she — context decides. She drinks tea is just as right.
mereka = they, and nasi goreng keeps its own order: rice-fried.
Verbs never take an ending for who is doing it.

steps.body: Indonesian glues a subject straight onto an adjective or a place. There is no verb in between.
steps.title: Drop "am, is, are"

steps.why: Nothing stands in for "am". capek is the casual word for tired.

steps.body: adalah exists, but it is formal and only links two nouns. Put it before an adjective and the sentence breaks.
steps.title: adalah is formal, and noun-to-noun only

steps.why: adalah never sits in front of an adjective — besar needs no link at all.

steps.body: "This coffee" is kopi ini — literally "coffee this". On their own, ini and itu mean "this" and "that".
steps.title: ini and itu come after the noun

steps.why: Noun, then ini, then the adjective. No "is".
di = at or in, and the "is" is simply absent. Going to would be ke kantor.

steps.body: Every describing word follows its noun. Read them backwards into English and they click.
steps.title: Noun first, describer second

steps.why: air = water, dingin = cold, and cold comes second.
The describer follows: rice-fried.

steps.body: Owners sit after the thing owned, and you can stack them. For friends and family, -ku and -mu attach straight to the noun.
steps.title: Possession follows too

steps.why: Stack the owners after the noun: motor – teman – saya.
es = ice, teh = tea, manis = sweet. The warung default, and it is very sweet.
-mu attaches to the end of the noun. nama kamu works too.

steps.body: Nouns don't change for plural. Context usually does the job: dua kopi is simply "two coffee". Add a number or a quantity word and you're done.

examples.en: There are lots of tourists here

steps.title: No plural ending

steps.why: With a number, the noun stays single. Doubling is never added on top of a number.

steps.body: Doubling a noun makes it plural with a sense of many or all sorts: anak-anak (children), buah-buahan (all kinds of fruit). Some doubled words simply have their own meaning, like kupu-kupu (butterfly) and jalan-jalan (going out for fun).

examples.en: The kids are playing on the beach
We want to go out and wander
examples.note: jalan-jalan = to go out for fun
a doubled word with its own meaning

steps.title: Doubling means "a variety of"

steps.why: banyak already says "many", so orang stays single.
semua orang = all people, everyone. suka = like.
beberapa = several, a few. Useful for "how long are you staying?".

steps.prompt: The kids are on the beach
steps.why: No verb needed for a location, and doubling gives "the kids".

units.title: The basic pattern

units.blurb: One little word in front of the verb does the work of every English tense.

steps.body: Verbs never change shape. You put a small marker in front instead: sudah (already / did), sedang (in the middle of), akan (will), belum (not yet).

examples.note: sedang is often shortened to lagi in speech

steps.title: Markers, not tenses

steps.why: sedang marks something going on right now. In conversation most people say lagi makan.

steps.body: Add a time word and the verb still doesn't move: kemarin (yesterday), tadi (earlier today), nanti (later today), besok (tomorrow).

examples.en: Yesterday I went to the market

steps.title: Time words carry the rest

steps.why: The time word can open the sentence or close it. pergi stays as it is.

steps.body: Asking whether someone has eaten is small talk, not an invitation. Answer sudah or belum and everyone is happy.
steps.title: "Sudah makan?" as a greeting

steps.why: belum = not yet, and it leaves the door open.
sudah + bayar. Nothing marks the past on the verb itself.
belum is the polite, optimistic "not yet". Tidak sounds like a refusal.

steps.body: Where English says a flat "no", Indonesian often says belum — not yet. It is the normal answer to anything that could still happen one day.
steps.title: belum keeps it open

steps.body: pernah marks experience: have you ever. With belum in front, it is "not yet ever".
steps.title: pernah = have ever

steps.prompt: "Pernah makan durian?" — you never have. Reply:
steps.why: belum pernah is what people actually say. bukan never touches a verb.

steps.body: lagi means "again", "more", and — in casual speech — "in the middle of" instead of sedang.
steps.title: lagi does three jobs

steps.why: lagi sits at the end for "more", and ya softens the request into a please.
Casual lagi = sedang. A friend texting you this means "what are you up to".
belum pernah + ke. No verb for "been" is needed.

steps.body: jam means both "hour" and "o'clock". Put the number after it. Add pagi, siang, sore or malam to show which part of the day.
steps.title: jam + number

steps.prompt: Your boat leaves at 9am. Which one?
steps.why: jam comes first for clock time. Sembilan jam means "nine hours", a length of time.

steps.body: setengah means half, and it counts towards the next hour: setengah empat is 3:30, not 4:30. Quarters use seperempat with lewat (past) or kurang (to).
steps.title: Half past is half to

steps.prompt: Someone says "setengah tujuh". What time is it?
steps.why: setengah counts towards the next hour: half (of the way to) seven.
jam + berapa (how many). Literally "hour how-many?".

steps.answer: We'll meet at five in the afternoon
options: We'll meet at five in the afternoon
steps.why: ketemu = meet (casual for bertemu). No future marker needed; the time says it.

steps.body: For a length of time, the number goes before the unit: dua jam (two hours), sepuluh menit (ten minutes). Ask with berapa lama.
steps.title: How long

steps.why: kira-kira = roughly. Number before jam for a duration.

steps.body: Time words are built from hari (day), minggu (week), bulan (month) and tahun (year), plus ini (this), depan (next, literally "front") and lalu (last).

examples.en: Next year I'm going to Java

steps.title: Today, this week, next month

steps.why: lalu = past, gone by. depan points forward.

steps.body: Days take hari in front: hari Senin, hari Selasa… In speech hari is often dropped. Minggu is also Sunday, so context tells you if it's a week or the day.
steps.title: Days of the week

steps.why: Time words can open or close the sentence. pulang = go home.
libur = day off, holiday.

steps.prompt: A friend asks when you arrived. You came three days ago:
steps.why: yang lalu after a length of time = ago. … lagi = in … time.
lagi after a length of time points forward: two more weeks.

units.title: Time without tenses

units.blurb: Two words for "not" — one for verbs and adjectives, one for nouns.

steps.body: tidak goes in front of what you are denying — an action or a quality.
steps.title: tidak for verbs and adjectives
